doc_summary: Carlini explains his motivation for writing attack papers and lays out a framework where disclosure timing depends on how patchable a vulnerability is, illustrated with case studies from web security to ML. He defends breaking others' defenses (e.g. Glaze) as necessary because defenses only matter if tested by an attack designed against them.

items.claim: prefers evaluating a defense against an attack built specifically for it over a generic benchmark because the only attack that matters is the one tailored to break that specific defense.
items.quote: There is no single benchmark for security. You can't just evaluate your defense on “the attack benchmark” and call it a day. Because the only attack that matters is the one that's designed to break your specific defense.

items.claim: Understand the system better than its builder to find exploits; deep system knowledge, not generic probing, is what surfaces real failures.
items.quote: The only way you'll come up with an exploit is by understanding the system better than the person who built it in the first place! Because they (presumably) aren't aware of any exploits

items.claim: prefers publicizing a vulnerability class over only fixing the specific instance because the underlying class will not be resolved by patching individual bugs and others need to learn from it.
items.quote: When a vulnerability is not just a single bug, but an instance of a new class of bugs, it's important to go public with it so that others can learn from it and not make the same mistakes in the future.

items.claim: prefers attacking things that are both interesting and important over forcing work he doesn't care about because intrinsic interest drives productivity.
items.quote: If you can find something that (a) you're interested in and (b) is important to do, you'll be far more productive than trying to force yourself into doing something that you don't care about.

items.claim: Distrusts defenses whose protection can't be updated after deployment, since a later break retroactively compromises everything already released.
items.quote: Once someone has published their adversarially noised images, they've lost control of them---they can't update them after that. And someone who wanted to train a model on these protected images only needs to download a bunch of images all at once, wait a few weeks or months for an attack on the defense

items.claim: Choose what to test and how to act by locating the vulnerability on the patchable-to-unpatchable spectrum, which determines disclosure and urgency.
items.quote: Identifying where a given vulnerability lies on the spectrum is important because it helps to determine how you should disclose the vulnerability.

items.claim: prefers publishing an attack because the vulnerability is likely to be independently rediscovered over withholding it because a less benevolent finder might exploit it.
items.quote: Someone else was bound to be able to re-discover this attack, and if we didn't go public with it, then the next person to discover it might not be so nice and just sit on it to exploit it for their own gain.

items.claim: Real-world context (actual deployment and usage) changes how carefully findings should be handled, as ML moved from unused to ubiquitous.
items.quote: But a lot has changed since 2018. Most importantly: machine learning models are now used everywhere. And so that means that now, when we discover attacks, we're considerably more careful about how we disclose them.

items.claim: Give the target's authors a chance to check the attack for errors before publishing, to ensure the evidence is correct.
items.quote: We did provide Ben's group with an initial draft of the paper to make sure they could check any errors in our work, but it doesn't make sense to wait for a patch

items.claim: prefers doing the adversarial work others avoid over leaving it undone because defenses can't be fixed unless someone shows they are broken.
items.quote: It may be true that attacking things is easier than defending them, but if no one else is going to attack then I'll be happy to be the one who does.
